nutshell: Multi-modal object ReID (fusing RGB, near-infrared, and thermal-infrared images of the same person/vehicle) is hurt by irrelevant background regions, both within each modality and as extra noise when aggregating across modalities. EDITOR extracts tokens with a shared ViT, uses a Spatial-Frequency Token Selection (SFTS) module to keep only object-centric tokens (via attention-based spatial selection plus a wavelet-based frequency selection), aggregates the selected tokens across modalities with a two-stage Hierarchical Masked Aggregation (HMA), and adds two new losses that explicitly use the discarded background tokens (BCC) and per-identity feature centers (OCFR) to further suppress background influence.
contributions: Spatial-Frequency Token Selection (SFTS): combines an attention-rollout-based spatial token selection (union of top tokens across attention heads, then across modalities) with a frequency-based selection that sums Discrete Haar Wavelet Transform decompositions across modalities and inverse-transforms them into one shared saliency map, to pick object-centric tokens each modality/instance individually.

Hierarchical Masked Aggregation (HMA): a two-stage aggregation - independent per-modality masked self-attention over the selected tokens, followed by a collaborative stage that concatenates all three modalities' aggregated tokens and runs a second masked-encoder pass to fuse them.

Background Consistency Constraint (BCC): rather than simply discarding the non-selected 'background' tokens (as prior token-selection ReID work does), an MSE loss aligns these background tokens pairwise across modalities, using background consistency as an explicit training signal instead of wasted computation.

Object-Centric Feature Refinement (OCFR): per-identity, per-modality moving-average feature centers that are pulled together via an MSE loss, encouraging tighter same-identity clustering after background suppression.
Near/state-of-the-art mAP on RGBNT201 (multi-modal person ReID), RGBNT100 and MSVR310 (multi-modal vehicle ReID), reported with fewer parameters than the closest competitor, TOP-ReID.
deficiencies: On RGBNT201 - the paper's own person-ReID benchmark and arguably the most central use case - EDITOR is clearly beaten by TOP-ReID's stronger 'A' setting (72.3 vs. 66.5 mAP, 76.6 vs. 68.3 Rank-1, roughly a 6-point mAP gap); the paper only claims a win over TOP-ReID's weaker 'B' setting (65.7 vs. 64.6 mAP) and explains away the larger loss with an unverified hypothesis ('potentially addressing the modality laziness problem') rather than any supporting analysis.

In the paper's own ablation (Table 2), the titular Spatial-Frequency Token Selection module contributes a modest +1.5 mAP (60.7→62.2, model B→C), while simply adding the HMA aggregation module to the raw baseline already contributes +6.7 mAP (54.0→60.7, model A→B) - the paper's headline 'Magic Tokens' selection idea does noticeably less work than the aggregation module it's paired with.

Table 4 shows frequency-based selection alone actually underperforms spatial-based selection alone (64.1 mAP / 65.3 R-1 vs. 65.0 / 66.8), and combining them adds only +0.7 mAP over spatial-only (65.7 vs. 65.0) - the 'frequency' half of the paper's core architectural contribution has negative standalone value in the reported numbers and a marginal combined contribution, despite being one of two named components in the paper's title.

The claimed efficiency advantage ('EDITOR has fewer parameters than TOP-ReID, making it more efficient') is asserted in the RGBNT201 discussion but never substantiated anywhere in the main paper - no parameter count, FLOPs, or latency table is given for either method.

All results across all three benchmarks are single-run point estimates with no variance/confidence reporting, and on the smallest benchmark (MSVR310, explicitly described by the authors as small-scale with complex scenarios) the margin over the next-best competitor CCNet is a few points (39.0 vs. 36.4 mAP) with no repeated-run evidence it's stable.
notable: The frequency-based token selection is a genuinely distinct, non-learned idea worth knowing about: it sums per-band Haar wavelet decompositions across all three modalities and inverse-transforms the combined result into a single cross-modal saliency map, giving a cheap way to fuse structural/edge information across modalities without any learned parameters - potentially reusable as a lightweight fusion prior elsewhere. Also worth flagging: TOP-ReID, the strongest competing method EDITOR is benchmarked against throughout (and loses to under setting 'A'), shares overlapping authorship with EDITOR (Yuhao Wang, Pingping Zhang, and Huchuan Lu appear as authors on both papers) - not disqualifying, but worth knowing when weighing how independent that particular comparison is.
